## My data

The Fairness dataset contains hospital patient data.Each row is one patient and ther are r scales::comma(nrow(fairness))rows.

ThThe Sports dataset contains sumo wrestler records from 1957–2023. Each row represents one appearance of a wrestler in the Makuuchi Banzuke division, and the dataset contains r scales::comma(nrow(sports)) rows. The data come from the SCORE Sports Data Repository. 【1-094996】


##References 
SCORE Network. (2023). Sumo wrestler characteristics. SCORE Sports Data Repository. https://data.scorenetwork.org/wrestling/sumo_wrestingling_since_1957.html

Fairness dataset. (2026). Dataset provided for CIS-3901 Guided Project, Catawba College

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Which scale, and why? What does a reader see with it
that they wouldn't see without it? If values were removed (0 or below on a
log scale), say how many.

I used a log scale because the data are spread out. It makes the pattern easier to see, and values of 0 were removed because a log scale cannot show zero.

### A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3
#| ref.label: a3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same rates in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "Two faceted bar charts showing readmission rates by gender across racial groups, with one using fixed y-axes and the other using free y-axes."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-chosen
#| include: false
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3
#| tbl-cap: "Each group's n and rate, by panel."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(a3_rates, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (3–4 sentences): Fixed or free? What does the reader gain, and what do
they lose? Which panels or groups are small, and what is their n? Describe
differences, not causes.

I chose the fixed version because it makes the panels easier to compare. The reader can quickly see differences between groups because all panels use the same scale. Smaller groups have lower n values, which are shown in the panel labels. The plot shows differences in readmission rates across groups, but it does not explain why those differences exist.

WRITE (2–4 sentences): Explain your colors. Say which column you colored by
and why. If your first choice failed the color check, say what you changed:
fewer categories, grouping rare ones, or panels. Then look at your simulated
plot: can you still tell the categories apart?

I colored the plot by gender to compare the two groups. I used a color-blind-friendly palette so the colors are easy to distinguish. The gender labels also help identify the groups without relying only on color. Yes, I can still tell the categories apart in the simulated plot.

The plot shows the relationship between wrestler weight and the number of wins. The axis labels help a reader the most because they clearly show what is being compared.

### B2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| ref.label: b2

```

```{r}
#| label: b2-check

```

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Which scale, and why? If values were removed, say how
many.

I used a log scale for wrestler weight because it makes the data easier to read. The log scale helps show the overall pattern in the data more clearly. No values were removed.

### B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-b3
#| ref.label: b3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same plot in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "Two faceted scatterplots showing the relationship between wrestler weight and wins for different heya groups, using fixed and free y-axis scales."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: b3-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (3–4 sentences): Fixed or free? What does the reader gain, and what do
they lose? Which panels are small, and what is their n? Differences, not
causes.

I chose the fixed version because it makes the heya groups easier to compare. The reader gains a consistent scale across all panels, but loses some detail that may be easier to see with free scales. The smaller panels have lower n values, which are shown in the panel labels. The plot shows differences between heya groups, but it does not explain the causes of those differences.

### B4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b4
#| ref.label: b4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels showing wrestler weights for wrestlers with winning and losing records, including individual values and resampled means."
```

```{r}
#| label: b4-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Do the clouds overlap? What does that say about
individuals versus the group means?

The clouds overlap quite a bit between the two groups. This suggests that many individual wrestlers have similar weights. The group means are more stable and show less variation than the individual values.

## One thing I tried in my slides, and why

WRITE (2–3 sentences): One idea of your own in your slides (an angle, a
comparison, an order, an annotation), and how it helps a reader see the
finding.

One thing I tried in my slides was presenting the faceted readmission rate chart before discussing its limitations. This helped readers see the differences between groups first and then think about the sample sizes and limitations. The order made the main finding easier to understand.
